template: Tonight, name one moment today when fear chose for you. What did it cost, and what would the braver version have looked like?
Where are you currently calling something prudence that is really avoidance?
Pick the conversation you have been postponing. When I next have ten free minutes today, I will send the first message that opens it.
When I notice my stomach tighten before speaking in a group today, I will say the thing anyway, in one sentence, before the moment passes.
Imagine the feared outcome arriving exactly as you picture it. Describe, plainly, what you would do the next morning. Most of the terror lives in the not-picturing.
Who taught you what courage looks like in ordinary life, and which of their habits have you quietly stopped copying?
Review the day as a ledger of small repetitions. Which one, repeated for a year, would you be glad about — and which would you regret?
What did you do today purely because it was already your routine, and did it still deserve the slot?
When I sit down at my desk tomorrow morning, I will spend the first fifteen minutes on the work that compounds, before opening anything that pings.
Choose one habit to shrink to something absurdly small. When today's usual cue arrives, I will do the two-minute version rather than skip it entirely.
Stop treating today as a test of willpower. Treat it as a question about design: which single obstacle, removed tonight, would make tomorrow's version happen by default.
Where else in your life is the pattern {text_short} already true, and what does that older success tell you about starting this one?
Tonight, review the day as {author} might: which hour was spent as if time were infinite?
If this month were the last one you were given notice of, what would you stop doing tomorrow morning?
Pick the task you keep deferring to a someday that never dates itself. When I sit down at my desk today, I will spend the first twenty minutes on it.
When I catch myself saying we should catch up sometime today, I will stop and propose an actual date before the sentence ends.
You are not short of time; you are spending it on things you would not choose twice. List the three largest line items of yesterday and mark which you would buy again.
Whose remaining time are you assuming is unlimited, and when did you last act as if it were not?
Before bed, name three ordinary things that went right today and would have been badly missed had they gone wrong. Which did you not notice at the time?
What did you complain about today that a version of you five years ago would have counted as a win?
When I finish reading this, I will send one person a specific thank-you for something they did months ago and probably assume you forgot.
When I sit down to my first meal today, I will pause for the length of one breath and name where the food and the money for it came from.
Imagine losing, for one week, the thing you complained about most this month. Write what that week would actually contain. Then return it to the ledger as an asset.
Which person is currently doing something for you so reliably that you have stopped seeing it — and what would it take to say so?
Tonight, replay a single sentence you said today that shaded the truth in your favour. Why did that shading feel necessary?
Where today did you behave differently because someone was watching, and which version was the real one?
When I am next tempted today to say yes to something I intend to quietly not do, I will say a plain no instead and give the real reason.
When I notice myself softening a fact in an update today, I will send the unsoftened version and let the discomfort be short.
Assume the person you are managing an impression for already knows the truth and is waiting to see whether you will say it. Nothing about the day changes except your next sentence.
Where does {source} demand more of you than your current standard does, and what would closing that gap cost this week?
Where was your mind today while your body was somewhere else, and which moment would you most like to have actually been inside of?
What did you look at today for long enough to actually see?
When someone starts telling me something today, I will put the screen face down and let them finish before I begin composing my reply.
When I next reach for my phone out of habit rather than need today, I will spend that minute looking out of the nearest window instead.
Your attention is not being stolen; it is being spent, mostly by you, in very small denominations. Reread the day as a bank statement rather than a robbery report.
Which part of your life is currently getting the leftovers of your attention, and who else notices before you do?
Tonight, review your day's conversations: in which one were you more interested in being understood than in understanding?
Which relationship in your life is running on stored credit rather than recent deposits?
When I have a spare five minutes today, I will message the friend I keep meaning to contact and ask one real question rather than a generic greeting.
When the next disagreement starts today, I will say back what the other person meant, in their words, before I say what I think.
Assume the person who annoyed you this week is fighting something you know nothing about, and that they would say the same of you. Re-run the exchange on that assumption.
Who in your life most needs to hear this idea from {source} — and why is it true for them?
Tonight, name the hardest part of the day: what did it demand of you that easier days never ask for?
Which past difficulty, now finished, are you still describing as though you did not survive it?
When the current problem next feels immovable today, I will write down the single smallest next action and do only that, then stop.
When I catch myself rehearsing the unfairness of a setback today, I will spend that same energy asking who has solved this before and how.
Read the obstacle as the assignment rather than the interruption to it. What does the day look like if this difficulty is precisely the work, and not in the way of the work.
What did an earlier version of you learn from a hard season that you are refusing to apply to this one?
What did you make today, however small, and what did the making teach you that consuming would not have?
Where did you stop short of the version that would have been good, and what were you protecting?
When I open my laptop today, I will make the ugly first version of the thing before I read anyone else's finished one.
When the work feels stuck today, I will set a timer for twenty minutes and deliberately produce something bad, on the understanding that it will be thrown away.
Treat the blank page as a supply problem rather than a talent problem. You are not short of ability today; you are short of raw material and permission to waste some of it.
Whose work taught you what care looks like in {theme_name}, and which of their standards have you let slip?
Tonight, find one thing you were confidently wrong about today. What would it have taken to notice at the time?
Where did you speak past the edge of what you actually know today, and who was in the room?
When someone corrects me today, I will say thank you and ask a follow-up question instead of explaining why I was nearly right.
When I am asked something I only half know today, I will say I do not know and offer to find out, rather than filling the silence.
Consider that the person you find least impressive in the room understands something about the situation that you do not. Spend one conversation today finding out what.
Which strongly held opinion of yours has survived only because you never went looking for its best opponent?
Tonight, ask what today's work was ultimately for. If the honest answer is momentum, what would you rather it were for?
Which of your current ambitions did you actually choose, and which did you inherit without inspecting?
When I plan tomorrow tonight, I will put one task that serves the ten-year version of my life at the top, above everything merely urgent.
When I am next offered something flattering but off-course this week, I will decline it in one sentence and name what I am protecting instead.
Imagine finishing everything currently on your list and feeling nothing. Take that seriously for a moment, then ask what was missing from the list rather than from you.
How does the idea {text_short} change what you would say if a stranger asked what you are working towards?
What did you spend today — money, hours, or attention — on something you would not miss if it vanished tomorrow?
Which of your current wants would look absurd to you if you already had it?
When I next open a shopping page today, I will add the item to a list dated a month from now instead of to a basket.
When I have ten minutes free this evening, I will remove one object, one subscription, or one recurring commitment that no longer earns its place.
Price things in hours of your life rather than in currency. Recalculate the last purchase you hesitated over, and the last one you did not hesitate over at all.
What did you once badly want, get, and stop noticing — and what does that pattern predict about your current list?
Tonight, replay the moment your temper moved today. What was the gap between the event and your reaction, and what happened inside it?
Which irritation did you carry all day that had already ended by mid-morning?
When the first frustrating message arrives today, I will name the feeling to myself before replying, and let ten minutes pass before I send anything.
When I feel my voice rise in a conversation today, I will lower it deliberately and ask a question instead of pressing the point.
Assume the driver, the colleague, the delay have no opinion of you whatever. Nothing today was aimed. Re-read the morning with the personal insult removed and see what is left.
What does the thing that angers you most reliably reveal about what you are quietly protecting?
Who was made better off by your day, and would they be able to name what you did?
Where did you give today while keeping a private account of it, and what were you hoping to be repaid with?
When I see someone struggling with something I am good at today, I will offer specific help rather than a general let me know if you need anything.
When I finish my work today, I will spend fifteen minutes on something that helps someone else and that they will never trace back to me.
Stop asking whether you can afford to give this away and ask what it is currently costing you to hold. Attention, expertise and introductions all spoil in storage.
Who gave you something unrepayable, and who is currently in the position you were in then?
What did you learn today that you could explain to someone else tomorrow, and what did you merely read?
When did you last change your mind about something that mattered, and what actually did it?
When I finish the next thing I read today, I will close it and write three sentences from memory before looking back at the text.
When I hit something I do not understand today, I will stay with it for ten more minutes before searching for someone else's summary.
Treat the confusion as the signal rather than the failure. The passage you had to reread is the only part of the day that was actually teaching you anything.
Which idea from {source} contradicts something else you believe, and which of the two have you examined less?
Which decision did you carry unmade through the whole day, and what did carrying it cost in attention?
What are you currently calling research that is really a way of not choosing?
When I next find myself weighing the same two options today, I will set a five-minute timer, pick one, and write down what would have to be true to revisit it.
When I open my list tomorrow morning, I will do the first hard thing on it before the three easy ones, even badly.
Most decisions are reversible and are being priced as though they are not. Sort today's open choices into the few that are doors and the many that are only corridors.
Where has waiting for certainty served you well, and where has it only ever cost you the option?
Tonight, read this back slowly. What in your day would look different if you had believed it fully this morning?
Which part of this do you already agree with in principle and consistently ignore in practice?
What made you save this in the first place, and is that still the reason it matters?
Turn this into one concrete commitment. When the next relevant moment arrives today, I will act on it once, in a way I could describe to someone else tonight.
When I plan tomorrow this evening, I will place one task on the list that exists only because of this idea.
When I catch myself doing the opposite of this today, I will stop mid-sentence, name it out loud or in writing, and choose again.
Imagine the day going wrong in the exact way {text_short} warns about. Describe what you would do next, plainly and without drama.
Argue the opposite for two minutes as though you believed it. Whatever survives that is the part of this idea you can actually rely on under pressure.
Where else in your life is this already true, and what does that older example suggest about applying it here?
Who would disagree with {author} about this, and what would their strongest objection be?
